label: 1930s
title: The Last Night at Villa Bellavista
premise: Autumn, nineteen thirty-four. An easterly gale lashes the Mediterranean coast and cuts off Villa Bellavista, the country retreat of the industrialist Alonso Valdés, in the middle of a weekend party. Between the gramophone, the champagne and a road washed out by the rain, someone will not live to see the dawn.

motives: Had forged signatures on Hilaturas Valdés promissory notes worth a fortune. {victim} had found out and meant to lay it before the court the next day.
Had sold the plans for the new looms to a rival mill in Sabadell. {victim} had the proof and meant to hand it to the Civil Guard the next day.
Had concealed an earlier marriage, made in Buenos Aires and never dissolved. {victim} had obtained the certificate and meant to make it public the next day.
Had run down a labourer on the coast road and driven off without stopping to help. {victim} knew the truth and meant to tell the magistrate the next day.
Had hidden contraband arms in the bales of cotton arriving at the port. {victim} had found out and meant to report it the next day.
Had blackmailed half of Valencian society with stolen letters. {victim} had found the hiding place and meant to expose the blackmail the next day.

arrivals: The taxi crawls along the coast road at walking pace, its wipers fighting the downpour. Round the last bend Villa Bellavista appears, white and ablaze with light on the cliff, while the sea bursts against the rocks. At the gate, a lantern swings in the wind.

You step off the train at a deserted station that smells of brine and coal. A black motorcar carries you between pines bent by the easterly to the villa, where a gramophone still plays behind the windows. The gravel crunches under your sodden shoes.

The telephone dragged you from your bed, the line full of crackles and a voice begging discretion. Now you pass through the gates of Villa Bellavista, your coat soaked through and the roar of the storm in your ears. For an instant, lightning sketches the palms and the white façade.

You cover the last stretch on foot, for the flood has cut the lane a few yards from the house. From the front steps you can hear the piano, the wind and, far below, the sea. Someone opens the door before you can knock.
tensions: The road is cut and the telephone line all but dead. Nobody will leave this house before dawn, and whoever did it knows that as well as you do.
In the music room, the gramophone has kept turning without music, the needle scraping at the end of the record. The guests eye one another over their glasses. One of them is lying.
Outside, the storm gives no quarter; inside, the lamps flicker with every thunderclap. You have until it abates to sort the secrets from the truth.

night: The rain beats harder against the panes and, somewhere in the house, a maid is murmuring the rosary.
The gramophone falls silent at last. There remain only the wind in the shutters and the creaking of the house, groaning like an old ship.
The electric light flickers and dies for a moment; the butler hands out candles along the corridors without a word.
A thunderclap rattles the mirrors. The guests no longer feign conversation: they smoke in silence, eyeing one another.
The candles have burnt halfway down. The sea strikes the cliff with greater fury than ever, and the telephone gives a shrill ring that nobody dares answer.
The gusts come further apart, and the silence they leave is worse than the noise. Nobody sleeps: everyone is waiting for the road to open and the Civil Guard to come up.
epilogues: You gather everyone in {scene} while the butler closes the doors one by one. When you have finished, nobody looks at {culprit}, but everyone steps back a pace. {culprit} offers no resistance, asking only to sit by the window, and watches the rain, which falls feebly now. At dawn the storm retreats out to sea, and up the newly opened road come the patent-leather tricorns of the Civil Guard. As {culprit} is led out to the car, the butler puts out the lamps of the house, one by one.

There is no need to raise your voice. You set out the facts one after another, and {culprit}'s hands begin to tremble, until at last the gaze drops. The butler, unbidden, takes up his place by the door. For a long while nobody speaks; there is only the rain, ever fainter. At first light, a pair of Civil Guards climb the front steps, their capes streaming. The sergeant hears your account, nods, and asks {culprit} to come along. Behind, in the villa, someone puts on a record again, very softly, as if to bid the night farewell.

In {scene}, before them all, you go over the night step by step and end with the name of {culprit}. For a moment there is only the wind. Then {culprit} sits down very slowly, as though the whole body had suddenly grown heavy, and the butler brings a glass of water that nobody drinks. When the easterly drops and the sky over the cliff turns pearl grey, the headlamps of the Civil Guard climb between the pines. You step out onto the terrace to breathe salt and wet earth: {victim} will give no more orders in this house, and Villa Bellavista wakes in silence.
